meaning: A vocabulary-sized vector of zeros with a single 1 marking the word. Every pair of different words has cosine similarity 0, so nothing learned about one word transfers to another.

A short dense vector (typically 100–300 numbers) learned for each word so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors. Looking one up equals multiplying a one-hot vector by the embedding table.
Words that appear in similar contexts have similar meanings: “you shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth, 1957). The idea behind word2vec and GloVe.
Mikolov et al.'s 2013 family of shallow models (skip-gram and CBOW) that learn word vectors by predicting which words appear near which, trained on billions of words.
word2vec's task of predicting each surrounding word from the centre word within a window. Slower than CBOW, better for infrequent words.
Continuous bag of words: predict the centre word from the average of its surrounding words. Faster than skip-gram.

Replace a softmax over the whole vocabulary by 1 real (word, neighbour) pair pushed towards σ = 1 and k random 'fake' pairs pushed towards σ = 0, so a step costs k + 1 dot products. Without negatives all vectors collapse together.
Global Vectors (Pennington et al., 2014): count word co-occurrences once, then fit vectors so their dot products match the log counts; ratios of co-occurrence probabilities become vector differences.
Vector arithmetic like king − man + woman ≈ queen. It works partly because standard code excludes the input words from the answers; allowing them sharply lowers accuracy.
A word vector computed from the whole sentence (ELMo, BERT, LLMs), so “bank” by a river and “bank” with money get different vectors. Static embeddings give one vector per word.
A network that reads a sequence one step at a time and updates a hidden state: h_t = tanh(W h_{t−1} + U x_t + b). The same weights are used at every step, so it handles any length.
The fixed-size vector an RNN carries from step to step: its running summary (memory) of everything read so far.
Training an RNN by unrolling it into one layer per time step (shared weights) and running ordinary backprop; the shared weights' gradients are summed over steps.
Carry the hidden state forward across chunks of K steps but stop the gradient at chunk boundaries. Bounds memory and adds updates, but the gradient can't teach dependencies longer than K.
The gradient from k steps back is a product of k factors W·tanh′; when they are below 1 it shrinks exponentially (0.5²⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶), so a vanilla RNN can't learn long-range dependencies.

A gated recurrent cell (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) with a separate cell state updated additively, c = f⊙c + i⊙g, and output h = o⊙tanh(c). Along the cell state the gradient is multiplied only by the forget gate.
The LSTM's memory 'conveyor belt': changed only by multiplying with the forget gate and adding gated new content, so information and gradients can travel many steps.
A sigmoid 0–1 valve that scales the old cell state each step (Gers et al., 2000). Initializing its bias to about 1 or more makes the cell start by remembering.
tools: PyTorch packs LSTM gates as [i, f, g, o]

meaning: A sigmoid output between 0 and 1 multiplied element-wise with a signal, letting the network learn how much to let through (forget, input, output, update, reset gates).

Cho et al.'s 2014 lighter gated cell: an update gate z keeps the old state and fills 1 − z with a new candidate; a reset gate controls how much old state the candidate uses. Three weight blocks instead of the LSTM's four.
One network reads the input sequence into a representation, a second generates the output sequence from it, so input and output lengths can differ (translation).
In a plain encoder–decoder the whole source must fit in one final state; translation quality degrades rapidly as sentences get longer.

For each output step, score every encoder state with v·tanh(W s + U h), softmax the scores into weights, and take the weighted average (the context vector). Removes the bottleneck; the weights act as a learned alignment.
The attention-weighted average of encoder states that the decoder reads for one output step.
Training a decoder by feeding it the correct previous token rather than its own prediction. Stable and parallel-friendly; causes exposure bias.
The mismatch between training on true prefixes (teacher forcing) and generating from the model's own outputs, so early mistakes can derail the rest.
Decoding that keeps the B most probable partial outputs at every step instead of only the single best word (greedy); usually with length normalization.
A small filter of shared weights slid along a sequence; over word vectors a width-k filter is a learned k-gram detector. All positions are computed in parallel.
Keep each filter's largest response over all positions, turning any-length text into a fixed-size vector (one number per filter).
A convolution whose output at time t only uses inputs at t and earlier (pad on the left only), so it can be used to generate sequences.
A filter that reads inputs d steps apart. Doubling d per layer doubles the receptive field per layer: 1 + (k − 1)·Σd, e.g. 1,024 samples for WaveNet's 10-layer block.
A stack of dilated causal 1D convolutions with residual blocks used as a general sequence model; parallel and gradient-stable, but its memory is fixed by the receptive field.
